name: Daria Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. It's confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you honestly think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior stockperson at Kestrel Hill Farm, which is three hundred outdoor sows plus maize and barley, run by Petra and Jan Novak. I start at half six walking the paddocks, checking the farrowing huts, topping up feed and water, and fixing whatever the pigs have wrecked overnight. In the afternoon I might be on the tractor or doing the pig movement records. I've been there a year and a half, and pigs still outsmart me most days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the piglets, obviously, and I like that Petra lets me try things. Last spring I set up ear-tag sensors on twenty sows so we can see when they're about to farrow. The hard part is the mud in winter and that the pay is basic. I rent a small flat in the market town, I've got about four months of costs saved, and I sell eggs from my own thirty hens online for extra.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask it about sow health, it drafts the movement records, and it checks the pig prices for Petra. I also used it to build my egg shop page in an evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still really useful, just not magic. I'd post something like that on the farming forum I'm on. At work I'd tell Jan he was right not to buy that robot feeder last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. My job's safe, Kestrel Hill is doing okay, and the little AI tools still save me an hour a day on records. It just means my growth comes from my own effort, not from riding a big wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the records and the egg shop, and I'd get another forty hens to grow the egg business. I'd ask Petra if I could run the sensor tags on the whole herd. Savings stay where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A little disappointed, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the egg shop bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and twenty a month after feed, which is the difference between going out on Friday and not. With seventy hens it could be two hundred and fifty. I've already got the spare coop from Petra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the sensors on the whole herd do for Kestrel Hill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer dead piglets, mainly, because you'd be at the hut when the sow starts. Last winter Kestrel Hill lost a litter of piglets at three in the morning because nobody knew the sow had started. If the sensors had been on that sow, I'd have been there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge chance for small farms if they're smart about it. I'd post about the sensors and the egg shop as examples. At work I'd tell Petra we should be first, not last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. The thinking tasks, like ordering feed, booking the haulier and doing the paperwork, move to software, and I'm the one who already runs it. Robots come slowly to outdoor pigs, because mud and pigs break everything. So I'd become the person who runs the systems while still doing the stock work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up an AI feed-ordering system for Kestrel Hill this winter and ask for a pay rise when it saves money. I'd double the egg shop and add pork boxes from Petra's pigs. I'd put five hundred of savings into a second-hand incubator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting. A bit like the first warm day in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kestrel Hill would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jan, a little. He does the feed ordering and the money side by phone and paper, and he's proud of it. If I set up the system, I'd have to do it without making him feel pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said mud and pigs break everything. Would you still bet on robots coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not soon, no. Outdoor pigs are about the last place a robot wants to be. But the day a robot can survive a sow in a bad mood, I'll be the first to buy one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and anyone who says they saw it coming is lying. I'd post that small farmers need to share what works fast. At work I'd tell Petra we need a plan this month, not next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the first picture that makes me nervous. In 2028 the AI does everything I'm proud of: the records, the ordering, the sensor reading. Then around 2031 the robots can walk the paddocks, so my stock work goes too. I'd be thirty with skills that a machine does better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before the robots, I'd go where the robots go. I'd apply to the farm-robot companies as a field specialist, the person who helps farmers set them up, because I know both pigs and software. I'd push savings to six months. And I'd keep the egg shop running as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels anxious but busy. I'd be too occupied to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would leaving Kestrel Hill be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. Petra took a chance on me with no experience. But staying at Kestrel Hill to be replaced by a robot isn't loyalty, it's just slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would a field specialist job last, if the robots get better every year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe five years, maybe less. I know that. But I'd rather be inside the change, learning, than outside it, waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance to get ahead of it. I'd post a lot about how small farms can use the time. At work I'd ask Petra for a proper plan, with me helping run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay about it. The AI in 2031 takes the desk side, and robots come around 2034. That's seven years of being the person who knows how to run the new kit. I'd be thirty-four, maybe with a small place of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving for land, maybe renting ten acres for my own pigs within three years. I'd put AI and sensors on everything I own from day one. And I'd ask Petra about buying in as a junior partner if Kestrel Hill brings in robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, with a bit of nerves about how fast it might really move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten acres of your own pigs. Is that realistic on your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Renting is, yes. Ten acres near us rents for about two thousand a year. I'd start with ten sows and grow from the pork boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you nervous, if you feel mostly good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots. If robots can run a pig farm in 2034, then big companies will run huge ones cheaply. My ten acres would have to sell on story and taste, not price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should plan like it. I'd post about it on the forum: start your side business now, while there's time. At work I'd keep pushing Petra to modernise step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the best one for me. AI comes in 2036 and robots around 2039, and by then I'd be thirty-nine with my own pig unit running on robots I chose. Ten years is enough to learn the business side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time farm business course next year, rent land in two or three years, and grow the pork boxes to a hundred customers. I'd keep the job at Kestrel Hill while I build. Savings go to the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels great. Like having the whole season in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you give up on your own unit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the supermarkets started selling robot-farmed pork for half the price, I'd have to rethink. But people who buy my pork boxes want to know the pig had a name. That doesn't change because of a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about Kestrel Hill if you left to run your own place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grateful. I'd want Petra to be my first partner, sharing a robot or a haulier. Small farms need each other more than they need anyone else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything of your own before the robots come. What would help is cheap starter land for young farmers, and loans for small farms to buy the same kit the big ones get. Plain information too, so you know which robots actually work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what young farmers want. Most young farmers don't want to fight the robots. We want to own a few of them.

headlineQuote: Most young farmers don't want to fight the robots. We want to own a few of them.

She's **practical** about change and wants to own her own pig unit.
Only **AGI by 2028** makes her anxious; with time she plans to own **land**.
